extracted.intended_audience: energy sector professionals, utility and power company stakeholders, environmental policy and legal observers
extracted.subtask_description: A news summary of the Supreme Court's denial of emergency stay requests against the EPA's power-plant carbon rule, describing the legal reasoning, timeline considerations, rule requirements, parties involved, and possible administrative and political outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of success on the merits (stay standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the applicants have shown a strong likelihood of success on the merits as to at least some of their challenges to the Environmental Protection Agency’s rule.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Court-recognized factor for emergency relief — a showing that the applicants are likely to win on the underlying legal claims. Justice Kavanaugh agreed applicants showed a strong likelihood as to at least some challenges, which addresses one prong of the stay test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable harm (stay standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit is expected to make a decision in the case before compliance work needs to start in June, the applicants seeking the stay are unlikely to suffer irreparable harm without a stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court denied the emergency applications in part because applicants could not demonstrate irreparable injury in the interim; the timing of appellate review reduced the asserted need for immediate relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of appellate decision versus compliance obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit is expected to make a decision before compliance work needs to start in June, meaning applicants are unlikely to suffer irreparable harm without a stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical calendar considerations (when compliance begins vs. when an appeal will be decided) are material to whether an emergency stay is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule applicability and compliance requirements for covered plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the EPA’s rule issued in April, the owners of coal-fired and new gas-fired power plants set to operate past 2039 will be required to meet a carbon dioxide emission standard equal to installing a carbon capture and storage system and running it at 90% efficiency, with compliance beginning in 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language sets the substantive regulatory threshold (which plants are covered), the performance standard (CCS at 90%), and the compliance timeline (beginning 2032, affecting units operating past 2039).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine challenge to EPA authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants argued the EPA’s rule exceeded its authority under the major questions doctrine; opponents said that assertion is wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an agency action implicates the major questions doctrine — i.e., whether Congress clearly authorized the challenged large policy step — is a central merits issue in the litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious standard (APA review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents told the court the applicants’ challenge to the EPA rule was 'arbitrary and capricious' and that they cannot show success on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Administrative Procedure Act’s 'arbitrary and capricious' standard is invoked by parties on the merits to argue about the procedural and substantive reasonableness of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed harms: premature retirement and grid reliability impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants argued the EPA’s rule would cause the premature retirement of coal-fired power plants and would jeopardize the reliability of the nation’s electric grid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating concrete harms (economic, operational, reliability) from compliance is part of applicants’ case for emergency relief and for merits-based arguments about the rule's consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible administrative responses by the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a Trump administration, the EPA could ask the appeals court to remand the rule so the agency could rework it, or voluntarily implement an administrative stay of the rule while it reconsidered the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-litigation remedies and agency options (remand, voluntary stay, reworking the rule) are practical pathways that affect whether courts issue emergency relief and the litigation stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/administration control as a factor in litigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The outcome of the presidential election will likely affect the litigation over the EPA’s rule because a different administration might choose to continue defending the rule or to ask for remand/reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive branch’s expected posture toward defending or revising the rule influences the urgency and calculus of judicial relief and the practical future of the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition composition and breadth of challengers/opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of utilities, independent power producers, trade groups, 25 Republican state attorneys general, and industry associations sought the stay; opponents included major utilities and public power entities as well as environmental groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who files for emergency relief (size and composition of petitioning coalition) and who opposes it can signal the breadth of impacted interests and may influence courts’ perceptions of the dispute’s gravity and consequences.
